title: Structured Events Are the Building Blocks of Observability
subtitle: Keep one request’s context together
summary: Pip’s market logs contain all the right words but cannot connect them to one request. Structured events accumulate context during a unit of work and record its outcome. Wide fields keep combinations available for questions nobody thought to ask in advance.

concepts.title: An event represents a unit of work
concepts.body: Pip starts an event when a checkout enters the service. The chapter’s event represents that request’s interaction with the service. Route, tenant, selected backend, duration, and final status accumulate until completion. Pip keeps input, circumstances, and outcome associated instead of asking tomorrow’s investigator to guess their relationship.

concepts.title: Structure enables comparison
concepts.body: Pip stores “request took 820 milliseconds” inside a JSON message. Encoding prose as JSON does not structure the useful attributes. A numeric duration_ms field supports comparison; a tenant field supports grouping without parsing changing sentences. Pip gives machines stable named fields for the questions that matter.

concepts.title: Wide records retain combinations
concepts.body: Pip finds failures only for one rare build-region combination. A wide event retains many attributes of the same request. Joint context permits comparisons involving build, user group, and backend together. Separate aggregates can lose the association even when every individual total survives.

concepts.title: Enrich during execution
concepts.body: Pip does not know the account or chosen shard at request entry. Authentication, routing, retries, and errors reveal context during execution. Pip enriches the same event as those facts arrive. The final record explains what actually happened, including the outcome unavailable at the start.

misconceptions.claim: Any JSON log is automatically a useful structured event.
misconceptions.correction: A JSON wrapper around prose can still omit queryable fields and coherent request context.

misconceptions.claim: Separate counters for tenant and build preserve their relationship.
misconceptions.correction: Their independent totals do not reveal which tenant and build occurred together on each request.

scenario.title: A pile of disconnected logs
scenario.context: A service logs tenant, backend choice, and failure on separate lines without request identity.

options.label: Emit one enriched request event
options.benefit: Preserves the relationship among context and outcome.
options.cost: Requires collecting attributes through the request lifecycle.
options.consequence: Concurrent requests remain distinguishable because each record holds its own context.

options.label: Add more descriptive text to each line
options.benefit: Can improve readability for an individual message.
options.cost: Still leaves concurrent requests difficult to correlate.
options.consequence: The investigator must still guess which messages describe the same request.

scenario.debrief: The missing information is the relationship among facts, not the volume of prose.

quiz.question: Which event design best supports explaining a tenant-specific failure?
options: A counter for all errors and a separate list of tenants
One prose message with a timestamp
A request record joining tenant, route, build, duration, and outcome
quiz.explanation: The joined attributes preserve the combinations needed for later investigation.

quiz.question: Why continue enriching an event after request entry?
options: Execution reveals routing choices and outcomes that were not yet known
An exit-time record should replace the original routing context with final status
Later enrichment is mainly for reformatting the original message as readable text
quiz.explanation: A coherent record combines initial context with facts discovered during the work.

quiz.question: Which structured field supports meaningful numeric latency filtering?
quiz.explanation: A typed duration retains a value that can be compared and aggregated directly.
